gaps.text: In-line measurement of temperature at the measurement point with temperature sensor

Combining several spectroscopy methods (data fusion) (A combined ATR/Raman probe collects both spectra from the same small measurement spot, so the two methods see the same material. The two spectrometers must be synchronised to a common time step, and each spectral block keeps its own calibration and diagnostics. The fused model must beat the best single method on independent runs, otherwise the second instrument is not justified.)
The existing laboratory measurements are an adequate reference for checking the in situ pilot.

items.finding: The source says temperature sensitivity of OH bands is a severe drawback for measuring aqueous solutions in NIR and MIR, making tempered sample holders necessary.
items.how_it_applies: For O2 with MIR ATR in aqueous medium, temperature at the measurement point may need to be controlled or monitored; test whether temperature variation affects the spectra.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: This is a review statement, not a cell culture or in-line probe study; tempered sample holders are laboratory hardware and may not transfer directly to an in-line measurement point.

citation.quote: Additionally, the temperature sensitivity of the OH bands is a severe drawback for measuring aqueous solution in NIR and MIR, which makes tempered sample holders necessary [29].
citation.label: E03 ¶12

items.finding: The source says low-level data fusion is the simplest way to combine inputs by rearranging variables from different sources into one data matrix.
items.how_it_applies: For O3, if ATR and Raman spectra are combined, low-level fusion is a candidate approach to test; ensure the variables from each method are aligned.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: This is a review of PAT data fusion, not a cell culture ATR/Raman study; it does not address synchronisation or separate calibration blocks.

citation.quote: Low-level data fusion (LLDF) is considered the simplest method to achieve a combination of inputs. In this case, the data is rearranged into a new data matrix, where the variables coming from different sources are placed one after the other.
citation.label: E02 ¶31

items.finding: The source says instrument complementarity was not always sufficient to improve prediction of several CQAs in a Raman and FT-IR food study.
items.how_it_applies: For O3, combining ATR and Raman may not improve performance; require the fused model to beat the best single method on independent runs before accepting the second instrument.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: This is a food analytical study using Raman and FT-IR, not ATR/Raman in cell culture; the CQAs, matrix and process differ.

citation.quote: In some situations, instrument complementarity (not data complementarity) was not sufficient to improve the performance of predictive several CQAs, as shown by a Raman and FT-IR data based food analytical study [73].
citation.label: E02 ¶36

items.finding: The source says a continuous process at a fixed probe location can simplify model design, with validation relying on independent steady-state runs.
items.how_it_applies: For the in situ pilot, consider whether independent steady-state runs are needed as a reference in addition to existing laboratory measurements.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: This is a lithium recycling liquid-liquid extraction process, not cell culture; it does not compare laboratory measurements with in situ data.

citation.quote: In contrast, a continuous process at a fixed probe location is intended to operate in a steady-state window, which simplifies the model design: calibrations can be narrower and centered on the operational envelope, validation can rely on independent steady-state runs, and online monitoring focuses on drift and out-of-specification detection rather than resolving the rapidly changing composition.
citation.label: E01 ¶8
